title: Two London Pharmacists Jailed Six Years Each Over £1.3 Million NHS Fraud
excerpt: Jignesh Patel, 46, and Rahil Patel, 42, were sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on 16 October after 1,639 false prescriptions were used to obtain high-cost leukaemia drugs that were sold to wholesalers in Europe.
body:
• Jignesh Patel, 46, and Rahil Patel, 42, were each sentenced to six years in prison at Southwark Crown Court on Friday, 16 October 2026, over a £1.3 million NHS prescription fraud.
  • Investigators found 1,639 false prescriptions in the names of 24 GPs for 440 patients, covering 6,983 dispensed items between January 2015 and November 2017, the NHS Counter Fraud Authority said.
  • High-cost hospital drugs including Sprycel (dasatinib) and Noxafil (posaconazole), used in leukaemia treatment, were obtained through Wise Pharmacy in Edmonton and sold on by Actipharm Limited to wholesalers in Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Germany.
  • Anyone who suspects NHS fraud can report it anonymously on 0800 028 4060, the NHSCFA's 24-hour line; investigators will now pursue recovery of the lost funds under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.

Two London pharmacists have been jailed for six years each for a prescription fraud that cost the NHS more than £1.3 million. Jignesh Patel, 46, was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court on Friday, 16 October 2026, and Rahil Patel, 42, received the same sentence at the same hearing, the NHS Counter Fraud Authority (NHSCFA) said. Both men had been found guilty on 6 October of three counts of fraud by false representation and two counts of converting criminal property, following a three-week trial at Southwark Crown Court.

"This was committed out of greed and you were equal partners in the serious fraud designed to make you a lot of money."

— His Honour Judge Cole, Southwark Crown Court

How the Fraud Worked

Jignesh Patel owned Wise Pharmacy at 93 Fore Street in Edmonton, north London, and also owned the pharmaceutical wholesale business Actipharm Limited. Rahil Patel worked at Actipharm, and at the time of the offences both men were the company's Responsible Persons — the role responsible for ensuring the conditions of its wholesale licence were complied with and for accurate record-keeping, the NHSCFA said.

https://x.com/DailyMail/status/2112857876377080173

The scheme centred on high-cost drugs that are normally dispensed in a hospital setting. Investigators identified seven such medicines dispensed by Wise Pharmacy that would not normally be expected in primary care: Sprycel, Noxafil, Atripla, Eviplera, Tobramycin, Truvada and Viread. The largest losses involved Noxafil (posaconazole) and Sprycel (dasatinib), used in the treatment of leukaemia. Examination of every prescription Wise Pharmacy dispensed between January 2015 and November 2017 found 1,639 false prescriptions written in the names of 24 GPs for 440 individual patients, totalling 6,983 dispensed items. The GPs named as prescribers confirmed they had not issued the prescriptions, and there was no documentation supporting any clinical need. The NHS reimbursed Wise Pharmacy more than £1.3 million for drugs listed on the false prescriptions.

Actipharm then sold the medicines on. Bank records showed a £28,900 payment from an EU pharmaceutical wholesaler for Noxafil, and sales of Noxafil and Sprycel to wholesalers in Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark and Germany; sales to the Netherlands and Germany alone totalled £779,405, according to the NHSCFA account, also reported by Chemist+Druggist. Text messages between the two men about obtaining false prescriptions and moving drugs, including "Drop the nox to the warehouse today" and "Get me the scripts from the scrip guys," formed part of the trial evidence.

How It Was Uncovered

The case began with anomalies in prescribing data across four London NHS clinical commissioning group areas — Barnet, Enfield, Newham and Tower Hamlets. The CCGs obtained copies of the prescriptions and checked them with the named GPs, who confirmed the drugs had not been prescribed. NHS England had alerted north London pharmacies in June 2016 that these specialist drugs were unlikely to be needed in primary care. After that alert, Wise Pharmacy stopped claiming reimbursement for Noxafil and Sprycel but continued obtaining them using stolen NHS prescriptions, investigators found.

Jignesh Patel was arrested on 6 December 2017 and gave a no-comment interview; £190,000 in cash was seized during searches of his properties. Rahil Patel was interviewed under caution on 14 February 2020 and also answered no comment. Evidence from European wholesalers was gathered through European Investigation Orders in the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium. At sentencing, Judge Cole praised the investigation as "thoroughly impressive" and "expertly presented on all sides."

What Happens Next

The NHSCFA said its investigators will now use their powers under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 to recover the lost funds. Jignesh Patel has also been reported to the General Pharmaceutical Council, Chemist+Druggist reported. Ben Harrison, the NHSCFA's Head of Operations and Engagement, said the investigation team "followed the evidence, both in the UK and Europe, to bring these individuals to justice," adding that "every pound stolen from the NHS is a pound that cannot be spent on frontline services." The authority's reporting line — 0800 028 4060, run with Crimestoppers — is the channel it asks the public to use for suspected fraud.
